title: Cloud basics, provider-agnostic
blurb: Load balancers, object storage, managed databases, CDNs, DNS, TLS and containers: what they are and why a CRUD app uses them, in any provider's vocabulary.

questions.q: What is the difference between a DNS A record and a CNAME record?
choices: An A record is only for the root domain; a CNAME is for every subdomain beneath it
An A record points at a server; a CNAME points at one port on that server for a service
An A record is cached by browsers; a CNAME is never cached, so changes apply at once
An A record maps a name to an IPv4 address; a CNAME maps a name to another name
questions.why: A CNAME says "resolve that other name instead", which is how you point `www` at a provider hostname that may change IP. It cannot sit at the zone apex alongside other records, which is why providers offer ALIAS/ANAME records. AAAA is the IPv6 equivalent of A.
questions.asked: Comes up whenever you connect a domain to a hosted service; the apex limitation is the follow-up.

questions.q: You will move your domain to a new load balancer's IP next week. What should you do with the record's TTL beforehand?
choices: Raise it to a week, so resolvers keep the old address until the move is complete
Lower it a day or more in advance, so cached answers expire soon after you switch
Leave it alone, since resolvers always re-check the authoritative server on a change
Set it to zero after switching, which pushes the new address out to every resolver
questions.why: Resolvers cache the record for the TTL they last saw, so the lower TTL must be in place for at least one old TTL before the switch. Changing it afterwards does nothing for answers already cached. Keep the old endpoint running for stragglers.
questions.asked: A migration-experience question; people who have done one talk about lowering TTL days ahead.

questions.q: Your load balancer is configured to terminate TLS. What does that mean?
choices: It closes any connection that has not finished its TLS handshake within a time limit
It passes the encrypted traffic straight through, so only the app holds the certificate
It holds the certificate, decrypts HTTPS, and forwards the requests on to the app
It stops accepting TLS versions older than 1.2 and rejects clients that still use them
questions.why: Terminating at the load balancer centralises certificates and lets it route on paths and headers, since it can read the request. Passing encrypted traffic through is TLS passthrough, the opposite. The app then learns the original scheme from `X-Forwarded-Proto`.
questions.asked: Checks that you know where HTTPS actually ends in a typical deployment.

questions.q: What can a layer 7 load balancer do that a layer 4 one cannot?
choices: Route by URL path, host or header, because it reads the HTTP request itself
Balance TCP connections across instances, which a layer 4 balancer cannot do
Handle UDP traffic, such as DNS or streaming video, alongside ordinary web traffic
Keep working when an instance fails, since layer 4 has no health checks at all
questions.why: A layer 4 balancer forwards TCP or UDP connections without looking inside, so it is fast and protocol-agnostic, and it does health checks too. A layer 7 balancer understands HTTP, so it can send `/api` to one pool and `/` to another, or add headers such as `X-Forwarded-For` for the app.
questions.asked: A common "do you know your infrastructure" question; path-based routing is the example to give.

questions.q: An instance behind a load balancer starts failing its health check. What does the load balancer do?
choices: Restarts the instance, then sends it traffic again once it has booted cleanly
Stops sending it new requests until the check passes again
Returns a 503 to every client until the failing instance recovers
Removes it permanently and launches a replacement from the latest image
questions.why: A load balancer only decides where traffic goes: it takes the instance out of rotation and puts it back when checks pass. Restarting or replacing instances is the job of an orchestrator or autoscaling group. The other instances keep serving, so clients do not see 503s.
questions.asked: Separates the load balancer's job from the orchestrator's, which candidates often blur.

questions.q: What does a CDN do for a web app?
choices: Hosts the app's database in several regions, so queries are answered locally
Compresses the app's JavaScript at build time, so the bundle is smaller
Replaces the load balancer, spreading requests across the app's instances
Caches content at edge locations near users, so requests travel less far
questions.why: A CDN serves cacheable responses from points of presence close to users and only goes back to your origin on a miss. That cuts latency and origin load. Build-time compression is your bundler's job; a CDN may compress on the fly, but it does not build.
questions.asked: A junior infrastructure check; the follow-up is what you must never let it cache.

questions.q: Compared with running your API on a VM you manage, what does a PaaS (a managed app platform) take off your hands?
choices: OS patching, the runtime install, and the deploy and scaling mechanics
Database schema design, since the platform generates tables from your models
Application bugs, since the platform restarts and patches your code for you
All security concerns, since the provider is responsible for the whole stack
questions.why: Under the shared responsibility model the platform owns the machine, OS and runtime; you still own your code, its dependencies, configuration and data. Restarting a crashed process is not fixing it, and your app's security holes remain yours.
questions.asked: Tests whether you know what you are still responsible for on a managed platform.

questions.q: Which workload suits serverless functions best?
choices: A WebSocket server holding thousands of long-lived connections open all day
A two-hour nightly batch job that keeps the CPU fully busy the whole time
Resizing images on upload, with traffic that arrives in unpredictable bursts
An API that keeps session data in process memory between separate requests
questions.why: Functions are short-lived, event-driven and billed per invocation, so bursty event work fits and idle time costs nothing. They have execution time limits, instances come and go (so no in-memory state), and long-lived connections are a poor match.
questions.asked: Checks whether you pick serverless for a reason, not because it is fashionable.

questions.q: What is a cold start on a serverless or scale-to-zero platform?
choices: The first deploy of a function, which must be approved before it can take traffic
A function failing because its database has not started yet after an outage
The delay while a new instance is created and your code loads before it can respond
The extra fee charged for the first request after a function has been idle for a while
questions.why: With no warm instance, the platform must start one and load your runtime and dependencies first, adding latency to that request. Smaller bundles, lighter start-up and a minimum instance count reduce it.
questions.asked: The follow-up is how you would reduce it; startup work and minimum instances are the usual answers.

questions.q: What is the difference between horizontal and vertical scaling?
choices: Horizontal splits the database by table; vertical splits it by rows across servers
Horizontal scales the frontend; vertical scales the backend and the database
Horizontal happens automatically; vertical always needs a manual restart
Horizontal adds more instances; vertical gives one instance more CPU and memory
questions.why: Vertical is simple but has a ceiling and usually a restart; horizontal needs a stateless app and a load balancer but also adds redundancy. Either can be automated. Splitting data is partitioning or sharding, a different topic.
questions.asked: A vocabulary check before any scaling discussion.

questions.q: Your autoscaler adds instances when CPU passes 70%, yet a sudden spike still causes errors for a few minutes. Why?
choices: Autoscalers only act on memory, so the CPU threshold is silently ignored
New instances take minutes to boot and pass health checks, so capacity arrives late
The load balancer sends traffic only to the original instances until a redeploy
CPU at 70% means the database is the bottleneck, so extra app instances do nothing
questions.why: Scaling is reactive: the metric must breach, the instance must boot, the app must start and pass health checks. Keep headroom with a higher minimum count, scale earlier or on request rate, schedule known peaks, and make start-up fast.
questions.asked: A production-experience signal; "autoscaling is not instant" is the insight.

questions.q: What is the difference between object storage and block storage?
choices: Object storage holds whole files by key over HTTP; block storage is a raw attached disk
Object storage is for structured rows; block storage is for unstructured files
Object storage is always slower, so it suits archives; block storage is for the app
Object storage lives in a single data centre; block storage is replicated across regions
questions.why: Object storage (S3, Blob Storage, GCS) stores and retrieves whole objects through an API and scales without limit; block storage is a volume your server formats and mounts like a local disk. User uploads go in object storage; a self-hosted database sits on block storage.
questions.asked: Leads into where uploads should live; knowing the access model is the point.

questions.q: What does a managed database service (such as RDS, Cloud SQL or Azure SQL) typically handle for you?
choices: Index design, since it adds an index for every slow query automatically
Schema migrations, which it applies whenever your application models change
Query tuning, since it rewrites inefficient SQL before running it for you
Automated backups, engine patching, and failover to a standby replica
questions.why: You pay for operations: backups, point-in-time restore, patching, monitoring and failover. Schema, indexes, migrations and query quality remain yours; some services suggest indexes, but none will design your data model.
questions.asked: Tests whether you know the line between the provider's job and yours.

questions.q: Someone runs a `DELETE` without a `WHERE` on the primary database. Why does the read replica not save you?
choices: Replicas store only indexes, not rows, so there is nothing to restore from them
Replicas copy every change, so the delete reached the replica within seconds too
Replicas are wiped whenever the primary restarts, which a large delete triggers
Replicas lag by a day, so they hold yesterday's data rather than the lost rows
questions.why: A replica faithfully copies mistakes as well as good writes. Replicas are for read scaling and availability; recovering from bad writes needs backups or point-in-time restore. "We have replicas" is not a backup strategy.
questions.asked: A classic trap: candidates who treat replicas as backups get this wrong.

questions.q: What does point-in-time recovery on a managed database let you do?
choices: Pause the database at a chosen time each night, so no writes happen during backups
Replay one table's changes into another table to undo a single bad transaction
Schedule a failover to the standby at a set time, for planned maintenance windows
Restore to any moment in the retention window, such as just before a bad migration
questions.why: The service keeps base backups plus the transaction log, so it can rebuild the database as it was at any second in the window, usually into a new instance you then copy data from. It restores the whole database, not one table.
questions.asked: Checks that you know how you would recover from a bad migration before you need to.

questions.q: Your managed database fails over to its standby in another availability zone. What does the app typically experience?
choices: Nothing at all; open connections move to the standby without any interruption
Dropped connections and errors for a short while, until it reconnects to the same endpoint
Permanent errors until someone edits the connection string to point at the standby's address
Loss of the last hour of data, because the standby is only refreshed from hourly backups
questions.why: The service repoints its DNS endpoint at the standby, which was kept in sync, so no committed data is lost. Existing connections break, though, so the app needs retries and a pool that discards dead connections.
questions.asked: Tests whether your app code is ready for the failover the provider promises.

questions.q: What is the difference between an image, a container and a registry?
choices: An image is a running app, a container is its saved snapshot, and a registry runs containers
An image is a VM disk, a container is the VM running it, and a registry is the hypervisor
An image holds only the configuration, a container holds the code, and a registry merges them
An image is a read-only template, a container is a running instance, a registry stores images
questions.why: You build an image once, push it to a registry, and every server pulls it and runs containers from it. Many containers can run from one image, each with its own writable layer that disappears when the container is removed.
questions.asked: Vocabulary that every deployment discussion assumes.

questions.q: What does a container orchestrator such as Kubernetes or ECS do for you?
choices: Builds your images from source and pushes them to the registry on each commit
Replaces your database with containers, so its data is replicated across nodes
Places containers on machines, restarts failed ones, and rolls out new versions
Writes a Dockerfile for each service from the language and framework it detects
questions.why: You declare the desired state (this image, three replicas, these resources) and the orchestrator keeps it true: scheduling, self-healing, rolling updates and service discovery. Building images is CI's job.
questions.asked: A mid-level awareness question; "desired state" is the phrase that shows you get it.

questions.q: Your app on a cloud VM needs to read from an object storage bucket. What is the recommended way to grant access?
choices: Create an access key for a service user and put it in the app's environment variables
Attach an IAM role or managed identity to the VM, which supplies short-lived credentials
Commit an access key inside an encrypted config file that the app decrypts at start
Make the bucket publicly readable, and rely on long random object names for privacy
questions.why: With a role or managed identity the SDK fetches temporary credentials from the platform and they rotate automatically, so there is no long-lived key to leak or rotate. Grant only the actions and bucket the app needs.
questions.asked: Tests whether your default is identities rather than keys, which is the modern baseline.

questions.q: What does a cloud secret manager add over putting secrets directly in the deploy configuration?
choices: Central storage with access control, an audit trail of reads, and managed rotation
Faster app start-up, because secrets are cached inside the container image at build
Encryption in transit, which environment variables set at deploy time do not have
Automatic detection of weak passwords, which it then replaces with stronger ones
questions.why: Secrets live in one place with per-app permissions, every read is logged, and database passwords can rotate without a redeploy. Baking secrets into an image is the thing to avoid: anyone who can pull the image can read them.
questions.asked: The follow-up is how your app picks up a rotated secret without downtime.

questions.q: Why is the production database usually placed in a private subnet?
choices: Private subnets have faster disks, which databases need more than app servers do
Traffic inside a private subnet is free, while public subnets are billed per query
It has no route from the internet, so only resources inside the network can reach it
Managed databases refuse to start in a public subnet unless encryption is disabled
questions.why: Defence in depth: even with a leaked password, an attacker on the internet cannot connect. The app tier reaches it inside the network, and security groups or firewall rules narrow that to the app only.
questions.asked: A network-basics question; the strong answer adds a security group allowing only the app tier.

questions.q: What is the difference between a region and an availability zone?
choices: A region is one data centre; an availability zone is a group of regions on one continent
A region is where you deploy; an availability zone is only where your backups are kept
A region is a geographic area; an availability zone is an isolated data centre within it
A region is billed per hour; an availability zone is a free replica of it for failover
questions.why: Spreading across zones in one region protects against a data-centre failure at low latency and modest cost (cross-zone traffic is billed). Multiple regions protect against a regional outage but bring data replication and much higher complexity.
questions.asked: Leads into "how available does this need to be?", which is the real design question.

questions.q: Background workers consume a queue whose backlog grows every afternoon. Which metric should the worker autoscaler act on?
choices: Average worker CPU, since more messages in flight always show up as higher CPU on the workers
Queue depth or the age of the oldest message, since that is the backlog users are waiting on
Requests per second on the web tier, since every web request eventually produces one message
Memory use on the workers, since a growing backlog is held in each worker's memory until processed
questions.why: The goal is to drain the backlog within a target time, so scale on the backlog itself: messages waiting, or better, how old the oldest one is. I/O-bound workers can sit at low CPU while thousands of messages wait, and memory says nothing because the backlog lives in the broker, not the worker. Web request rate is a proxy that ignores retries, bursts and slow consumers.
questions.asked: Shows you pick the signal that measures the user-facing problem; 'age of the oldest message' is the answer that marks real experience.

questions.q: You want `example.com` (the bare apex domain) to point at a managed load balancer whose IP addresses change. Why can't you use a normal CNAME at the apex?
choices: A CNAME at the apex is allowed, but browsers refuse to follow it over HTTPS connections to the site
The apex must also hold SOA and NS records, and a CNAME cannot coexist with other records
CNAME records only work for subdomains that are served over plain HTTP on port 80
The apex is cached forever by resolvers, so a CNAME there would never be refreshed
questions.why: The DNS spec forbids a CNAME alongside any other record at the same name, and the zone apex always has SOA and NS. Providers work around it with ALIAS/ANAME or 'CNAME flattening', which resolve the target server-side and answer with A/AAAA records.
questions.asked: Comes up the first time someone puts a site on a PaaS; knowing ALIAS/flattening shows you have actually done it.

questions.q: You updated a DNS record ten minutes ago. Your laptop sees the new address, but a colleague still gets the old one. What explains it?
choices: DNS changes propagate outward from the registrar in waves that always take a full 48 hours
The colleague's browser pinned the old certificate, which also pins the old address
Their resolver cached the old answer and will keep serving it until its TTL runs out
The authoritative server serves the new answer only to clients in the same region
questions.why: Nothing is pushed: each recursive resolver (and OS or browser cache) holds the answer for the TTL it received. 'Propagation' is just caches expiring at different times, which is why you lower TTLs before a change.
questions.asked: Tests whether 'DNS propagation' is understood as cache expiry rather than magic.

questions.q: Which DNS record type would you add to prove domain ownership to an email or certificate provider without affecting web traffic?
choices: An MX record with the verification token set as the mail server's priority value instead
A CNAME record on the apex that points at the provider's verification host
An A record for a `verify` subdomain that points at the provider's IP address
A TXT record holding the token the provider gives you, at the name it specifies
questions.why: TXT records carry arbitrary text and are what verification flows, SPF and DMARC use. Adding one changes no routing, whereas an apex CNAME is illegal and an MX would redirect mail.
questions.asked: Everyday task when wiring up email or a SaaS; shows you know which record does what.

questions.q: Your certificate from Let's Encrypt is valid for 90 days. What is the normal way to keep it from expiring?
choices: Automate renewal with an ACME client or the platform, renewing around day 60
Buy a paid certificate instead, since paid ones never need to be renewed at all
Set a calendar reminder and upload a freshly issued certificate by hand each time
Pin the certificate in the load balancer so clients ignore its expiry date
questions.why: Short lifetimes are designed for automation: an ACME client (certbot, Caddy, cert-manager, or the cloud's managed certificates) renews well before expiry. Manual renewal is exactly how certificates expire in production; paid certificates expire too, and lifetimes are shrinking industry-wide.
questions.asked: Expired certificates are a classic outage; interviewers want to hear 'automated, and alerted on'.

questions.q: One load balancer IP serves `api.example.com` and `shop.example.com`, each with its own certificate. How does it know which certificate to present during the TLS handshake?
choices: It reads the `Host` header of the first request and then restarts the handshake
The client sends the hostname in the ClientHello using SNI, before any HTTP is sent
It presents both certificates at once, and the browser picks the one that matches the URL
It cannot, so each hostname needs its own dedicated IP address on the balancer
questions.why: Server Name Indication puts the requested hostname in the ClientHello, so the server can choose a certificate before encryption starts. The `Host` header only arrives after the handshake, which is why one-IP-per-site used to be necessary before SNI.
questions.asked: Shows you understand the order of TLS and HTTP rather than treating HTTPS as one blob.

questions.q: Your login keeps users on the same backend instance using sticky sessions. What problem does this cause when you scale out or deploy?
choices: Sticky sessions encrypt the cookie, which makes the load balancer slower per request
New instances receive all traffic first, overloading them until the cookie expires
Load spreads unevenly, and users on a removed instance lose their in-memory session
Sticky sessions stop health checks, so a failed instance keeps receiving traffic
questions.why: Affinity pins existing users to old instances, so new ones sit idle, and anything held in instance memory vanishes when that instance is drained or crashes. Moving session state to a shared store (Redis, the database) or a signed token makes instances interchangeable.
questions.asked: Leads into 'make your app stateless'; the strong answer names where the session should live instead.

questions.q: During a deploy, the load balancer removes an old instance. What does connection draining (deregistration delay) do?
choices: It kills open connections immediately so clients reconnect to a healthy instance
It copies the old instance's memory to the new one so sessions survive the move
It pauses the deploy until every user of that instance has logged out of the app
It stops new requests going to the instance but lets in-flight ones finish first
questions.why: Draining takes the target out of rotation for new requests while giving existing requests a grace period to complete, which avoids 502s mid-deploy. Your app should also handle SIGTERM by finishing work rather than exiting at once.
questions.asked: Zero-downtime deploys depend on it; strong answers pair it with graceful shutdown in the app.

questions.q: Your API runs behind an L7 load balancer. What should the health check endpoint it calls typically verify?
choices: That the process is up and able to serve, with a cheap check that returns fast
That every downstream service and third-party API responds within a second
That the full test suite passes against production data on every single probe
Nothing at all, because a TCP connection succeeding is a better health signal
questions.why: The balancer probes every few seconds, so the check must be cheap and reflect whether this instance can serve. Making it depend on every downstream means one flaky dependency marks all instances unhealthy at once, turning a partial outage into a total one.
questions.asked: Probes whether you know deep health checks can cause cascading failure.

questions.q: One L7 load balancer serves your SPA and your API. Which rule sends `/api/*` to the API service and everything else to the static site?
choices: A DNS rule that returns a different IP address for URLs beginning with `/api`
A path-based listener rule matching `/api/*` that forwards to the API target group
A TCP port rule, because the browser carries each URL path on a separate port of its own
A CORS rule on the balancer that allows `/api` requests through to the backend
questions.why: Layer 7 balancers see the HTTP request, so they can route by path or host to different target groups. DNS never sees the path, and a TCP (L4) balancer cannot distinguish paths on one port.
questions.asked: Basic architecture for a same-origin SPA plus API, which also sidesteps CORS.

questions.q: You deploy a new SPA build, but users keep getting the old `index.html` from the CDN for an hour. What is the usual fix?
choices: Give `index.html` a hashed filename so the CDN treats every deploy as a new page
Put the whole site on a one-year cache and ask users to hard-refresh after deploys
Serve `index.html` with a short or no-cache policy and hashed assets with a long one
Disable the CDN for the entire site so that every single request goes to the origin server
questions.why: The entry HTML must be revalidated so it can point to new bundles, while content-hashed JS/CSS can be cached for a year because their names change on every build. You cannot hash `index.html`'s name, since the URL `/` must stay stable; an invalidation on deploy is the belt-and-braces addition.
questions.asked: Very common production confusion; the strong answer splits caching policy by file type.

questions.q: What does a CDN use to decide whether two requests can be served the same cached response?
choices: The client's IP address, so each user gets their own copy of the cached object
The response body hash, which the CDN compares after fetching from the origin
The TLS session ID, which ties each cached response to one encrypted connection
A cache key, normally the host and path, plus any query or headers you configure
questions.why: The cache key decides what counts as 'the same' request. Including too little (ignoring a query parameter that changes the response) serves the wrong content; including too much (every cookie) destroys the hit rate.
questions.asked: Leads to real bugs such as one user's personalised page served to everyone.

questions.q: A personalised `/account` page was accidentally cached by the CDN and shown to other users. Which response header prevents that?
choices: `Cache-Control: private, no-store`, so shared caches never store the response
`Cache-Control: public, max-age=0`, so the CDN revalidates the page every time
`Vary: Accept-Encoding`, so each user gets a separately compressed copy of it
`Expires` set to a date in the past, which the CDN reads as 'cache per user'
questions.why: `private` forbids shared caches such as CDNs and proxies from storing the response, and `no-store` forbids storing it at all. `public, max-age=0` still permits the CDN to store it, and `Vary: Accept-Encoding` splits by compression, not by user.
questions.asked: A real data-leak incident pattern; interviewers want the exact directive, not 'turn caching off'.

questions.q: Users upload profile photos. What is the common cloud pattern that keeps large files from passing through your API servers?
choices: Base64-encode the image in a JSON body and let the API write it to local disk
The API issues a short-lived presigned URL and the browser uploads directly to storage
Make the bucket publicly writable so the browser can upload directly with no credentials at all
Store the image bytes in a database column and serve it through the API later
questions.why: A presigned URL grants one upload to one key for a few minutes, so the browser talks to object storage directly and your API only records the key. A public-write bucket lets anyone fill it, and proxying big files through the API ties up instances and memory.
questions.asked: Standard system-design building block; strong answers mention expiry, size limits and content-type checks.

questions.q: Your app serves private invoices stored in object storage. How should a logged-in user download one?
choices: Make the bucket public but give files long random names that cannot be guessed
Put the storage account key in the frontend so the browser can fetch any file
After checking authorisation, redirect to a presigned GET URL that expires soon
Copy the file to the web server's disk on login so the user can download it
questions.why: The API authorises the request, then hands out a URL valid for one object for a few minutes; the bucket stays private. Unguessable names on a public bucket leak through logs, referrers and shared links, and a key in the frontend grants access to everything.
questions.asked: Checks you keep authorisation on the server even when storage serves the bytes.

questions.q: Your bucket fills up with temporary export files that nobody deletes. What is the storage-native fix?
choices: Enable versioning so older copies of each export are cleaned up automatically
Switch the bucket to a cold storage class so storing the exports costs nothing
Write a cron job on a VM that lists every object each night and deletes old ones by name
Add a lifecycle rule that expires objects under the `exports/` prefix after N days
questions.why: Lifecycle rules let the storage service delete or transition objects by prefix, tag or age with no code to run. Versioning does the opposite, keeping more copies, and cold tiers are cheaper, not free, with retrieval fees and minimum durations.
questions.asked: Shows cost awareness and knowledge that storage services manage retention for you.

questions.q: What does enabling versioning on an object storage bucket protect you from?
choices: An overwrite or delete, since earlier versions of the object can be restored
Someone reading an object without permission, since each version is encrypted
Running out of storage, since only the most recent version is ever billed
Region-wide outages, since each version is copied to a different region
questions.why: With versioning, an overwrite creates a new version and a delete adds a delete marker, so the previous data can be recovered. It does not control access or replicate across regions, and every retained version is billed, which is why you pair it with lifecycle rules.
questions.asked: Pairs with 'how do you protect against accidental deletion', a common reliability question.

questions.q: A serverless function opens a new Postgres connection per invocation. Under a traffic spike the database starts refusing connections. What is the usual fix?
choices: Raise the function's memory setting so each invocation can hold more connections
Put a connection pooler (PgBouncer or the provider's proxy) between them
Switch the database to a larger disk, which raises its connection limit in step
Retry connection errors in a tight loop until the database accepts the request
questions.why: Each concurrent function instance holds its own connection, so hundreds of instances exceed `max_connections`. A pooler multiplexes many client connections onto a few server ones; retrying in a loop only adds load, and disk size does not set the connection limit.
questions.asked: A classic serverless-meets-relational-database failure; knowing about poolers signals production experience.

questions.q: Your managed database provider announces a weekly maintenance window. What should you expect and plan for?
choices: Nothing, since managed databases patch themselves live with zero impact on open connections
A full restore from the previous night's backup, losing that day's writes
A brief failover or restart, so the app must reconnect and retry transient errors
Read-only mode for the whole window, so writes must be queued in the frontend
questions.why: Minor version patches and host maintenance usually mean a failover or restart lasting seconds to a minute. Apps that retry transient errors and let the pool rebuild connections ride through it; apps that cache one connection forever crash.
questions.asked: Checks you know 'managed' does not mean 'never restarts', and how to build for it.

questions.q: You write to the primary and immediately read from a read replica, but the new row is missing. Why?
choices: Replicas only receive changes once a night, during the scheduled backup window
Replicas reject reads for rows written in the last minute to avoid dirty reads
The write failed silently on the primary and was only recorded in the log
Replication is asynchronous, so the replica can lag the primary by some time
questions.why: Most replicas apply changes asynchronously, typically milliseconds but sometimes seconds under load. Read-your-own-writes paths (showing a user what they just saved) should read from the primary or wait for the replica to catch up.
questions.asked: Introduces eventual consistency with a concrete bug; strong answers route critical reads to the primary.

questions.q: Why must a web app deployed to a PaaS or container platform avoid writing uploaded files to its local disk?
choices: The local filesystem is ephemeral and per-instance, so files vanish or diverge
Local disks are read-only on every platform, so the write throws an exception
Writing to disk is slower than any network call, so it hurts response times
Local files are publicly served by default, which exposes every user's upload
questions.why: Instances are replaced on each deploy, restart or scale event, and each instance has its own disk, so a file written on one is invisible to the others and lost later. Object storage or a shared volume is the durable place.
questions.asked: The 'stateless app' principle in its most concrete form; a common junior-to-mid filter.

questions.q: A PDF export takes 10 minutes. Why is a serverless HTTP function a poor fit for running it inside the request?
choices: Serverless functions cannot write any files, so a generated PDF could never be saved anywhere
Functions and gateways have execution and response timeouts, often well under that
Serverless platforms bill per request, so a long request costs nothing extra
Functions run on one CPU, which makes PDF generation impossible to finish
questions.why: API gateways commonly cap requests at tens of seconds and functions have their own maximum duration. Long work belongs in a queue-triggered job or container task, with the request returning 202 and a status URL.
questions.asked: Leads to the async job pattern; strong answers mention 202 Accepted and polling or a webhook.

questions.q: Your app scales to zero overnight, and the first morning request takes eight seconds. Which change directly removes that delay?
choices: Adding a CDN in front of the API so that the first request is served from cache
Raising the request timeout so the first request does not fail while it waits
Setting a minimum instance count of one so a warm instance is always ready
Moving the database closer to the app so the first query returns more quickly
questions.why: The delay is a cold start: pulling the image, booting the runtime and warming up. Keeping one instance warm (min instances, provisioned concurrency) trades a small fixed cost for no cold start; a longer timeout just lets users wait.
questions.asked: A cost-versus-latency trade-off question; say what it costs as well as what it fixes.

questions.q: In your deployment manifest, why is referencing an image by digest (`myapi@sha256:...`) safer than by tag (`myapi:latest`)?
choices: Digests are compressed, so the image downloads faster onto every node
Tags are private to your registry, while digests work across every registry
Digests force the registry to rebuild the image from source on every pull
A digest is immutable, while a tag can be moved to a different image later
questions.why: Tags are mutable pointers: `latest` or even `1.4` can be re-pushed, so two nodes can run different code under the same name. A digest identifies exact content, making deploys reproducible and rollbacks precise.
questions.asked: Reproducible deploys; the strong answer also mentions immutable tags such as the git SHA.

questions.q: Your GitHub Actions workflow deploys to the cloud. What is the modern alternative to storing a long-lived access key as a repository secret?
choices: OIDC federation, where the cloud trusts the workflow's short-lived identity token
Committing the key to a private branch that only the deploy workflow ever checks out
Emailing the key to the workflow at runtime so it never touches the repository
Using the root account key, which is rotated by the provider automatically
questions.why: With OIDC the CI job requests a signed token, and a cloud role configured to trust that repository and branch exchanges it for temporary credentials. Nothing long-lived exists to leak, and the trust can be scoped to one repo and environment.
questions.asked: Shows you are current on CI security; strong answers mention scoping the trust to branch or environment.

questions.q: What does the principle of least privilege mean for your API's cloud role?
choices: The role gets administrator rights, but only during office hours when staff are on
Grant only the actions and resources the API actually uses, such as one bucket
Give every service the same role so permissions stay consistent across the team
Deny everything by default and let developers approve each call when it happens
questions.why: If the API is compromised, the attacker gets exactly what its role can do. Scoping to specific actions on specific resources (read and write on `uploads-prod`, not `s3:*` on `*`) limits the blast radius; a shared role spreads it.
questions.asked: Foundational security vocabulary; the strong answer ties it to blast radius.

questions.q: Your API instances in a private subnet need to call a third-party payment API on the internet. What typically provides that outbound access?
choices: An internet gateway attached directly to each instance with a public address
A CDN, which forwards outbound requests from the API to external services
A NAT gateway in a public subnet that the private subnet's route table uses
A read replica in a public subnet that relays the outbound calls for the API
questions.why: A NAT gateway lets private instances start outbound connections while nothing on the internet can start one inward. Giving instances public addresses defeats the private subnet; a CDN handles inbound content delivery, not outbound calls.
questions.asked: Tests whether you understand inbound versus outbound in a VPC; strong answers mention NAT data-processing costs.

questions.q: What is the main difference between a security group and a network ACL in a typical cloud VPC?
choices: Security groups apply to the whole VPC, while network ACLs apply to one instance
Network ACLs inspect HTTP content, while security groups only check the port
Security groups are only for outbound traffic, and network ACLs for inbound
Security groups are stateful per resource; network ACLs are stateless per subnet
questions.why: A security group attaches to an instance or interface and automatically allows return traffic; a network ACL applies to a whole subnet and needs explicit rules both ways. Neither inspects HTTP content, which is a WAF's job.
questions.asked: A classic AWS-flavoured question; the provider-agnostic idea is instance firewall versus subnet firewall.

questions.q: How should the database's firewall rule be written so only your API instances can reach it on port 5432?
choices: Allow 5432 from the API's security group or subnet, not from `0.0.0.0/0`
Allow 5432 from everywhere and rely on the database password to keep people out
Allow all ports from the API's subnet so future services can connect as well
Block 5432 entirely and have the API connect through the public internet instead
questions.why: Referencing the API's security group (or its subnet range) means only those instances can open connections, and the rule follows autoscaling. Relying on a password alone exposes the database to scanning and brute force.
questions.asked: Defence in depth in one rule; interviewers want network restriction and credentials, not either/or.

questions.q: Your monthly bill shows a large 'data transfer out' charge. What usually causes it for a web app?
choices: Uploads from users into your bucket, which are billed per gigabyte received
Egress: bytes sent to the internet or across regions, such as unCDNed downloads
Traffic between instances in the same availability zone over their private IP addresses
Database reads, because every query result is charged as outbound traffic
questions.why: Providers usually charge little or nothing for ingress but bill egress to the internet and between regions or zones. Serving large files straight from origin or chatty cross-region calls add up; a CDN, compression and keeping traffic in one region help.
questions.asked: Cost awareness is increasingly expected of mid-level devs; egress is the surprise line item.

questions.q: Why do teams apply tags such as `env=prod` and `team=billing` to cloud resources?
choices: Tags change how resources are billed, giving tagged resources a lower rate
Tags control DNS routing, so traffic reaches the tagged environment only
Tags let you attribute cost, find owners and target policies or automation
Tags encrypt resources with a key that belongs to the team named in the tag
questions.why: Tags are metadata: cost reports group by them, people find who owns an orphaned resource, and policies or scripts can target `env=dev` for nightly shutdown. They do not change pricing, routing or encryption by themselves.
questions.asked: Hygiene question; strong answers mention enforcing tags through policy or IaC.

questions.q: A worker takes a message from a managed queue (SQS, Azure Service Bus, Pub/Sub) and crashes halfway through processing it. What happens to the message?
choices: It is lost, because the queue deletes each message as soon as it has been delivered once
It reappears for another consumer after the visibility timeout or lock expires
It is moved straight to the dead-letter queue after the very first failed attempt
It stays locked to the crashed worker until an operator releases it by hand
questions.why: The consumer must explicitly delete or complete the message; until then it is only hidden for the visibility timeout or lock duration, after which it is redelivered. That is what makes delivery at-least-once, and why dead-lettering happens only after a configured number of attempts.
questions.asked: The core mechanic behind every queue question; everything about idempotency follows from it.

questions.q: Your queue consumer sometimes processes the same 'send receipt email' message twice. Given at-least-once delivery, what is the right fix?
choices: Switch to a queue that promises exactly-once delivery for every kind of consumer
Lower the visibility timeout so a duplicate is delivered before the first finishes
Make the handler idempotent, for example by recording processed message ids
Process messages on a single worker thread so that no duplicates can occur at all
questions.why: Duplicates are part of the contract: a consumer can finish the work and crash before acknowledging. Recording the message or business id (unique constraint, 'already sent' flag) makes the second run a no-op. A single thread still sees redeliveries, and a shorter timeout causes more duplicates, not fewer.
questions.asked: Idempotency is the most important queue concept at mid-level; interviewers want the mechanism, not a product name.

questions.q: A message fails processing every time because its payload is malformed. What stops it blocking or looping forever?
choices: Setting the message retention period to zero so the queue drops it at once
Raising the visibility timeout to an hour so it is retried less often by consumers
Catching the exception and acknowledging it silently so the queue moves on
A max-receive count that moves it to a dead-letter queue for inspection
questions.why: After N failed receives the broker moves the poison message aside, where you can alert on DLQ depth, inspect it and redrive once fixed. Silently acknowledging throws away evidence and data; a longer timeout only slows the loop.
questions.asked: Real teams get paged by DLQ depth; strong answers mention alerting on it and redriving.

questions.q: When an order is placed, three services (email, analytics, stock) must each react. Which messaging shape fits?
choices: Publish one event to a topic, with a separate subscription or queue for each service
Put one message on a single queue and let the three services compete for it
Have the order service call each of the three services' HTTP APIs in sequence, one by one
Write the order to a shared table and have each service poll it every second
questions.why: Pub/sub fan-out gives every subscriber its own copy and its own retry and backlog, so a slow analytics consumer does not delay email. On a single queue, consumers compete and each message goes to only one of them.
questions.asked: Distinguishes queue (work distribution) from topic (fan-out), a common confusion.

questions.q: What are RPO and RTO in a disaster recovery plan?
choices: RPO is the replica count you keep; RTO is how many regions you can fail into
RPO is how much data you can afford to lose; RTO is how long recovery may take
RPO is the request rate you promise; RTO is the timeout on each request made
RPO is the backup retention period; RTO is the time a backup takes to be written
questions.why: Recovery Point Objective is measured backwards from the failure (minutes of lost writes you accept), and Recovery Time Objective forwards (how long until service is back). They drive the design: hourly snapshots cannot meet a five-minute RPO.
questions.asked: Standard vocabulary in design rounds; strong answers connect the numbers to backup and replica choices.

questions.q: Your nightly database backups have run successfully for a year. What is the most important thing still missing from the backup strategy?
choices: Encrypting the backups a second time with a different key held by another team
Moving every backup to cold storage on the same day so that they cost far less
Regularly restoring one into a test environment to prove it actually works
Taking backups hourly as well, even though nobody has asked for a lower RPO
questions.why: An untested backup is a hope, not a backup: restores fail on missing permissions, wrong versions or corrupt files, and you also learn how long a restore takes, which is your real RTO. The other options change cost or frequency without proving recoverability.
questions.asked: Interviewers love this; people who have lived through a failed restore always mention testing.

questions.q: Your app depends on three services, each with a 99.9% availability SLA, and fails if any one is down. Roughly what availability can you expect?
choices: 99.9%, since the combined system is only as weak as the weakest single service
99.99%, since having three services gives you redundancy against any failure
Exactly 100%, since each SLA refunds you for downtime so it does not count
About 99.7%, since serial dependencies multiply: 0.999 × 0.999 × 0.999
questions.why: When every dependency is required, availabilities multiply, so three nines each gives roughly 99.7%, around 26 hours a year. Redundancy raises availability only when components are alternatives, not links in a chain.
questions.asked: Tests whether you can reason about SLAs quantitatively instead of quoting one number.

questions.q: What does running your database in a multi-AZ configuration protect you against?
choices: The loss of one data centre, by keeping a synchronous standby in another zone
An entire cloud region going offline, by keeping a copy on another continent
Bad data written by the app, since the standby rejects writes that look wrong
Slow queries, since reads are split evenly between the primary and the standby
questions.why: Multi-AZ keeps a standby in another zone of the same region and fails over automatically if a zone fails. It replicates bad writes faithfully, does not survive a region outage, and the standby often serves no reads at all.
questions.asked: Separates high availability from backups and from multi-region DR, which candidates often conflate.

questions.q: What is envelope encryption, as used by cloud key management services (KMS, Key Vault)?
choices: Encrypting data twice with the same key, so a leaked copy is twice as hard to read
Data is encrypted with a data key, and that data key is encrypted by a master key
Putting every secret in a signed JSON 'envelope' that expires after one hour
Encrypting only the metadata of each file while the contents stay readable
questions.why: Bulk data is encrypted locally with a fast per-object data key; only the small data key is sent to KMS to be wrapped by a master key that never leaves the service. Rotating or revoking the master key controls access without re-encrypting terabytes.
questions.asked: Shows you understand what 'encrypted at rest with KMS' actually does under the hood.

questions.q: Your API sits on the public internet and gets a flood of requests trying SQL injection strings. Which managed service is designed to filter these at the edge?
choices: A NAT gateway, which blocks inbound requests that contain SQL keywords
A read replica, which absorbs attack traffic so that the primary stays healthy
A web application firewall with managed rules in front of the load balancer
A private DNS zone, which hides the API's address from the attackers entirely
questions.why: A WAF inspects HTTP requests and blocks known attack patterns, bad bots and abusive rates before they reach your app. It is a layer on top of, not a replacement for, parameterised queries in the code.
questions.asked: Defence-in-depth question; strong answers stress that the WAF does not excuse unsafe code.

questions.q: An autoscaling group scales on CPU. It keeps adding and removing instances every few minutes. What is this called, and what is the usual fix?
choices: Cold starting, fixed by keeping one warm instance running at all times in the scaling group
Throttling, fixed by raising the account's API rate limit with the provider
Draining, fixed by disabling connection draining on the load balancer
Flapping, fixed with cooldowns and a gap between scale-out and scale-in thresholds
questions.why: Scaling out drops average CPU, which triggers scale-in, which raises CPU again. Cooldown periods, a scale-in threshold well below the scale-out one, and scaling in more slowly than out damp the oscillation.
questions.asked: Shows operational experience with autoscaling rather than just 'it scales automatically'.

questions.q: Why do autoscaling APIs need to be stateless to scale horizontally?
choices: Any instance can serve any request, so instances can be added or killed freely
Stateless code runs faster on each request, which reduces the CPU per instance
Load balancers refuse to route traffic to instances that keep data in memory
Stateless APIs do not need a database, which removes the scaling bottleneck
questions.why: If no user data lives only in one instance's memory or disk, the balancer can send requests anywhere and scale-in loses nothing. State still exists; it lives in the database, cache or object storage that all instances share.
questions.asked: Foundational; the strong answer says where the state moved to.

questions.q: Batch jobs that can be interrupted and resumed run every night. Which pricing option usually makes them much cheaper?
choices: Reserved capacity for three years, paid up front for the batch fleet
Spot or preemptible instances, which are discounted but can be reclaimed
Dedicated hosts, which avoid sharing hardware with other customers
On-demand instances in the most expensive region, to finish more quickly
questions.why: Spot capacity is spare capacity sold at a large discount with short-notice reclamation, which suits restartable, checkpointed work. Reserved capacity pays off for steady always-on load such as the production database, not for a few hours a night.
questions.asked: Cost-awareness question; strong answers match the pricing model to the workload shape.

questions.q: A developer left a large test database running for three months. What guardrail would have caught it early?
choices: A lifecycle rule on the database that deletes it after thirty days of use
A read replica, which alerts the team when the primary is idle for a week
Budget alerts plus cost reports by tag, with owners reviewing anomalies
Putting the database in a private subnet so that it costs less to run
questions.why: Budgets with alert thresholds and anomaly detection flag unexpected spend within days, and tags tell you who to ask. Network placement does not change instance cost, and databases do not have object-storage-style lifecycle rules.
questions.asked: Every team has a story like this; interviewers want to hear a preventive process.

questions.q: Your API reads the database password from a secret manager on startup. The password is rotated. What must the app handle?
choices: Nothing, since the secret manager updates the password inside running processes
Rotation only happens during deploys, so the next release picks up the new value
The database keeps accepting the old password for a year after every rotation
Fetching the new value on auth failure or periodically, without a full redeploy
questions.why: A value read once at startup goes stale. Apps either refresh the secret on a schedule, re-read it when authentication fails, or rotation uses a dual-credential scheme so old and new both work during the overlap.
questions.asked: Rotation is where 'we use a vault' answers get tested; strong candidates describe the overlap window.

questions.q: What does Terraform's state file record?
choices: The mapping between resources in your code and the real resources it created
The full history of every change made through the provider's web console
The compiled binary of each provider plugin, pinned for reproducible runs
A copy of every secret in the account, so each plan can compare them and report any drift
questions.why: State links `aws_s3_bucket.uploads` to the actual bucket id and caches attributes so `plan` can compute a diff. It often contains sensitive values, which is why it is stored in an encrypted remote backend with locking, not committed to git.
questions.asked: The first thing anyone asks about Terraform; strong answers mention remote state and locking.

questions.q: Someone changed a security group rule in the cloud console, and `terraform plan` now wants to revert it. What is this called?
choices: State locking, where the console locks out Terraform until changes are merged
Drift, where the real infrastructure no longer matches the code
Tainting, where the resource is marked to be destroyed and recreated
Refreshing, where Terraform downloads new provider versions automatically
questions.why: Drift is manual or out-of-band change diverging from the declared configuration. The fix is to either codify the change or let apply revert it, and to restrict console write access in production so it stops happening.
questions.asked: Shows you understand why teams ban console changes once IaC is adopted.

questions.q: Why do teams run `terraform plan` in the pull request and `apply` only after merge?
choices: Plans are free while applies are billed, so reviewers keep plans to a minimum
Plan checks code style only, and apply is what actually validates the syntax
Reviewers see exactly what will be created, changed or destroyed before it happens
Terraform refuses to apply unless the plan was generated on a different branch from main
questions.why: The plan is a readable diff of real infrastructure changes, so a reviewer can spot 'destroy and recreate the database' before merging. Applying from the main branch through CI keeps one audited path to production.
questions.asked: Connects IaC to code review; the strong answer mentions catching destructive replacements.

questions.q: Compared with clicking resources together in a console, what is the main benefit of infrastructure as code?
choices: Resources defined in code are cheaper, because providers discount automation
It removes the need for any access controls, since the code is the permission
Infrastructure defined in code cannot fail, because it is validated on commit
Environments are reproducible, reviewable and versioned like application code
questions.why: Code gives you the same staging and production from one definition, pull-request review, history and rollback, and a way to rebuild after disaster. It does not change prices or prevent failed applies.
questions.asked: Entry-level IaC question; strong answers mention reproducible environments and review.

questions.q: Your cloud logging bill has tripled. What is the most common cause in a web app?
choices: Debug-level logging or per-request payload dumps left on in production
Log retention set to the default, which is always a single day of storage
Structured JSON logs, which the provider bills at three times the plain rate
Logging to stdout instead of to a file, which the provider charges extra for
questions.why: Managed logging bills by volume ingested and retained. Verbose levels, full request bodies and health-check noise multiply it quickly; sampling, dropping noise and sensible levels fix it. JSON versus plain text makes little difference per byte.
questions.asked: Observability costs are a real budget item; strong answers mention log levels and filtering at the source.

questions.q: Your metrics bill jumped after someone added a `userId` label to the request-count metric. Why?
choices: Metrics with labels are stored as logs, which are billed at a higher rate
Each unique label combination is a separate time series, so cardinality exploded
The provider charges per character in a label, and ids are long strings
Labels force every metric to be sampled once a second instead of once a minute by default
questions.why: Time-series databases store one series per distinct label set, so a label with 100,000 users creates 100,000 series. High-cardinality detail belongs in logs or traces; metrics labels should be bounded, like route and status code.
questions.asked: Cardinality is the classic metrics mistake; interviewers want the 'where does per-user detail belong' answer.

questions.q: What does a managed container service (ECS, Cloud Run, Azure Container Apps) do that a plain VM running Docker does not?
choices: It builds your image from source code, so you no longer need a Dockerfile
It gives each container its own dedicated physical server for isolation
It schedules, restarts, scales and rolls out containers across a fleet for you
It removes the need for a registry by copying images straight from your laptop
questions.why: The platform decides where containers run, replaces failed ones, scales on load and does rolling deploys. On a lone VM you own all of that, plus patching the host.
questions.asked: Tests whether you know what 'managed' buys you in the container world.

questions.q: Your container needs to read a secret and write to one queue. How do you grant it cloud permissions without baking keys into the image?
choices: Build the keys into the image at a secret layer that is stripped when pushed
Mount the developer's personal credentials file from their laptop at deploy
Pass the root account's keys as environment variables in the task definition
Attach a workload identity or task role scoped to that secret and that queue
questions.why: The platform injects short-lived credentials for the role the workload runs as (task role, managed identity, workload identity), and SDKs pick them up automatically. Image layers keep every file ever added, and personal or root keys break least privilege.
questions.asked: Same idea as instance roles, applied to containers; interviewers check you know the SDK finds them itself.

questions.q: Your API reaches managed object storage over the public internet via a NAT gateway, and the NAT bill is large. What is the usual fix?
choices: A private endpoint or gateway endpoint so traffic to the service stays internal
A CDN in front of the bucket so the API downloads files from the edge instead
Giving each instance a public IP so it can skip the NAT for every request
Moving the bucket to another region, where data transfer is billed less
questions.why: Service endpoints route traffic to the provider's own services over its private network, skipping NAT processing charges and the public internet. Public IPs on instances undo the private-subnet design, and cross-region traffic costs more, not less.
questions.asked: A real cost win that shows you know how VPC traffic is billed.

questions.q: What does a managed Redis service (ElastiCache, Azure Cache for Redis, Memorystore) typically NOT give you by default?
choices: A single endpoint the app connects to without knowing which node is primary
A guarantee that cached data survives every failover and restart intact
Automatic patching of the Redis engine during a maintenance window
Metrics on memory use and evictions in the provider's monitoring console
questions.why: Replication is asynchronous, and persistence settings vary, so a failover can lose recent writes. Treat Redis as a cache you can refill, not as the system of record, unless you have deliberately configured and tested durability.
questions.asked: Checks you do not treat a cache as a database; strong answers mention designing for cold cache.

questions.q: In cloud terms, what is a VPC (or VNet)?
choices: A virtual private computer, meaning one VM that is not shared with anyone
A VPN client that developers install to reach the provider's web console
A logically isolated private network, with subnets and routes, for your resources
A paid support plan that gives you a private chat channel to the provider's own engineers
questions.why: A VPC is your own address space in the provider's network, divided into public and private subnets with route tables and firewalls. Everything else (instances, databases, load balancers) is placed inside it.
questions.asked: Baseline vocabulary; interviewers expect you to sketch public and private subnets from it.

questions.q: Why does a cloud provider give each account service quotas (for example, a maximum number of vCPUs per region)?
choices: Quotas are the provider's billing tiers, and raising one moves you to a pricier plan
Quotas limit how much traffic the load balancer accepts before it starts rejecting
Quotas are a security feature that blocks access from outside the home region
Quotas protect shared capacity and you from runaway spend; you request increases
questions.why: Quotas cap resources per account and region to protect the platform and stop a bug or compromised key spinning up thousands of machines. They can block a scale-out at the worst moment, so check them before launches.
questions.asked: Surfaces operational maturity: hitting a quota during a traffic spike is a known outage cause.

questions.q: You want a staging environment that mirrors production. What is the most reliable way to keep them from drifting apart?
choices: Define both from the same IaC modules, with only sizes and names as variables
Clone production by hand each quarter using the console's copy feature
Point staging at the production database so the data never drifts apart
Deploy to staging only after production, so staging always catches up
questions.why: One definition parameterised per environment means differences are explicit and reviewable. Sharing the production database with staging is a data-safety hazard, and manual clones drift from the day after they are made.
questions.asked: 'Works in staging, breaks in prod' is usually drift; strong answers make the differences explicit.

questions.q: What does a managed load balancer's access log give you that your app's own logs may not?
choices: The full request and response bodies for every call, for replaying traffic
Requests that never reached the app, such as those rejected or timed out upstream
The database queries each request ran, joined to the client's IP address
A copy of each user's session cookie, so you can impersonate them later for load tests
questions.why: Balancer logs show every request at the edge with status, target and timings, including 502s and 504s where the app never logged anything. They do not contain bodies or database activity.
questions.asked: Debugging 5xx errors that the app never saw is a common scenario; this is where you look.

questions.q: Your team wants to move a static marketing site off a VM. Which cloud setup is simplest and cheapest?
choices: A managed Kubernetes cluster running an nginx container across three zones
A serverless function that reads each HTML file from disk and returns it
Object storage or a static hosting service with a CDN and a managed certificate
A pair of VMs behind a load balancer so one can be patched while the other serves
questions.why: Static files need no compute: storage plus CDN (or Netlify, Vercel, Static Web Apps, Cloudflare Pages) gives global caching and TLS for pennies. Clusters and VM pairs add cost and patching for no benefit.
questions.asked: Right-sizing question; interviewers want the simplest tool that fits.

questions.q: Under the cloud 'shared responsibility model', which of these is YOUR job when you run an API on a managed platform?
choices: Patching the hypervisor and the physical hosts that your instances run on
Securing your code, its dependencies, your IAM policies and your data access
Guarding the data centre doors and destroying failed disks from the hardware
Keeping the provider's global network backbone running between its regions
questions.why: The provider secures the cloud itself (hardware, facilities, hypervisors, managed-service internals); you secure what you put in it: code, configuration, identities and data. Most cloud breaches are customer-side misconfiguration, such as public buckets or over-broad roles.
questions.asked: Frames every cloud-security discussion; strong answers note that 'managed' shifts the line but never removes it.

questions.q: A partner will only accept webhooks from a fixed list of IP addresses, but your API's instances scale in and out. How do you give outbound traffic a stable IP?
choices: Assign an elastic IP to the load balancer, which also becomes the outbound source
Ask the partner to allow-list your domain name, since IP lists are deprecated
Route outbound traffic through a NAT gateway with a static public IP address
Pin the API to a single instance so its address never changes over time
questions.why: All egress from private subnets leaves via the NAT gateway's fixed address, so the partner allow-lists one IP however many instances run. A load balancer's address is for inbound traffic, and pinning to one instance removes scaling and redundancy.
questions.asked: A common integration requirement; knowing the NAT answer shows you understand egress paths.

questions.q: Your browser app uploads directly to an object storage bucket using a presigned URL, and the browser reports a CORS error. Where is the fix?
choices: In your API's CORS middleware, since the API issued the presigned URL
In the presigned URL itself, by adding a `cors=true` query parameter to it
In the browser, by setting `mode: 'no-cors'` on the upload request
In the bucket's CORS configuration, allowing your origin and the PUT method
questions.why: The browser is talking to the storage service, so that origin must return the CORS headers; configure the bucket to allow your site's origin, the method and the headers you send. Your API's CORS settings do not apply to another host, and `no-cors` makes the response unreadable.
questions.asked: Catches people who think CORS is configured 'on the frontend'; it is always the responding server.

questions.q: Premium videos are served through a CDN, and only paying users should be able to play them. What is the usual mechanism?
choices: Signed URLs or signed cookies that the CDN validates, issued by your app after auth
A secret path segment in the URL that only paying users are told about
Checking the `Referer` header at the CDN so that only your own pages can embed them
Disabling caching for premium files so each request reaches your app first
questions.why: The app authorises the user and issues a URL or cookie signed with a key the CDN trusts, with an expiry; the edge verifies the signature without calling your origin. Secret paths leak, `Referer` is trivially forged, and disabling caching defeats the CDN.
questions.asked: Extends the presigned-URL idea to the edge; strong answers mention expiry and key rotation.

questions.q: A serverless function in Node creates its database client at module scope, outside the handler. Why is that a common optimisation?
choices: Module-scope code runs at build time, so the connection is baked into the bundle
Warm invocations reuse the same execution environment, so the client is reused
Module scope is shared by every instance of the function across the region
The platform bills module-scope code at a lower rate than handler code
questions.why: An execution environment serves many invocations in turn, and module-level state survives between them, so expensive setup happens once per cold start. It is not shared across concurrent instances, so each instance still holds its own connection.
questions.asked: Shows you understand the serverless execution model rather than 'a fresh process per request'.

questions.q: A container platform sends SIGTERM to your API before stopping it during a deploy. What should your API do?
choices: Ignore it, since the platform will wait indefinitely until the process exits
Exit immediately with exit code 0 so that the new version starts as fast as possible
Stop accepting new requests, finish in-flight ones, close connections, then exit
Restart itself in place so the platform thinks the container is still healthy
questions.why: Graceful shutdown drains work inside the platform's grace period (often 30 seconds) before SIGKILL arrives. Exiting at once drops in-flight requests as 502s; ignoring it just means being killed mid-request later.
questions.asked: Zero-downtime deploys need the app's cooperation; interviewers want the drain sequence.

questions.q: You give a container 256 MB of memory, and it is repeatedly killed with exit code 137 under load. What is happening?
choices: The container is out of disk space, and 137 is the code for a full filesystem
The health check is failing, and 137 means the load balancer removed it
The image is built for the wrong CPU architecture and crashes on start
It exceeds its memory limit and the kernel OOM killer sends SIGKILL
questions.why: 137 is 128 + 9, meaning the process was killed with SIGKILL, and the platform's events usually say OOMKilled. Raise the limit, reduce memory use, or configure the runtime's heap (Node's `--max-old-space-size`, .NET's GC limits) to fit inside the container.
questions.asked: A very common container incident; decoding 137 quickly signals hands-on experience.

questions.q: For a CRUD app with users mostly in the EU, which factor most often decides the cloud region?
choices: Latency to users plus data residency rules such as GDPR data-location commitments
The region with the newest instance types, regardless of where the users actually are
The region that the developers' office is nearest to, for faster deploys
The cheapest region worldwide, since latency does not matter for CRUD apps
questions.why: Putting compute and data near users cuts round trips, and contracts or regulation may require personal data to stay in a jurisdiction. Price differences between regions exist but rarely outweigh 150 ms added to every request.
questions.asked: A practical design question; strong answers mention both latency and compliance.

questions.q: What does an API gateway (API Management, API Gateway, Apigee) typically add in front of your services?
choices: A database connection pool shared by every service behind the gateway
Cross-cutting concerns such as auth checks, rate limits, routing and API keys
Automatic generation of your business logic from the OpenAPI description you upload
A replacement for TLS, since the gateway encrypts the payloads itself
questions.why: A gateway centralises edge policies: validating tokens, throttling per client, request routing, versioning and usage analytics. It does not replace business logic or TLS, and it adds a hop and a component to operate.
questions.asked: Common in enterprise stacks; strong answers name a cost as well as the benefits.

questions.q: Which DNS routing policy sends each user to the region with the lowest network latency for them?
choices: Weighted routing, which splits traffic by the percentages you configure
Failover routing, which sends everyone to a primary until it is unhealthy
Latency-based routing, which answers with the endpoint measured fastest
Round-robin A records, which rotate the order on every resolver query
questions.why: Latency-based (or performance) routing uses the provider's measurements between resolver networks and regions. Weighted routing is for canaries and gradual migrations, failover for active-passive setups, and round-robin spreads load blindly.
questions.asked: Shows you know DNS can do more than map a name to one IP.

questions.q: You run a primary region and a standby region. How can DNS move traffic automatically if the primary goes down?
choices: Resolvers notice failed connections and pick another A record by themselves
Set the TTL to a week so resolvers keep a stable answer during the outage
Registrars move the domain to the standby region's name servers on failure
Use failover routing tied to a health check, with a short TTL on the record
questions.why: The DNS provider probes the primary and answers with the standby's address when checks fail; a short TTL makes clients pick up the change quickly. Long TTLs keep clients pointed at the dead region, and registrars do not react to outages.
questions.asked: Active-passive DR in one question; strong answers mention TTL and data replication to the standby.

questions.q: Why should a production database have deletion protection enabled, even when it is managed by Terraform?
choices: A mistaken `destroy` or a rename that forces replacement will be refused
Deletion protection makes backups run more often, which lowers the RPO
It encrypts the database so that deleted data cannot be read by the provider
Terraform cannot manage databases unless deletion protection is switched on
questions.why: Some attribute changes make Terraform destroy and recreate a resource; deletion protection (plus `prevent_destroy` in code) turns that into an error instead of data loss. It has no effect on backups or encryption.
questions.asked: A cheap guardrail against the scariest IaC mistake; mentioning it shows care.

questions.q: Two engineers run `terraform apply` against the same environment at the same moment. What prevents them corrupting the state?
choices: Terraform merges both plans automatically and applies them in alphabetical order
State locking in the remote backend, so the second run waits or fails
Git, since the state file is committed and conflicts show up at merge time
The cloud provider rejects any second change to an account within a minute
questions.why: Remote backends (S3 with locking, Azure Storage leases, Terraform Cloud) take a lock for the duration of a run. Committing state to git gives no runtime locking and leaks secrets; the better practice is applying only from CI.
questions.asked: Follows naturally from 'what is state'; interviewers want remote backend and locking.

questions.q: What is the main difference between Terraform and a tool such as AWS CDK or Pulumi?
choices: Terraform manages only networking, while CDK and Pulumi manage only compute
CDK and Pulumi apply changes without a preview, while Terraform always plans first
CDK and Pulumi let you describe resources in a general-purpose language such as C#
Terraform is imperative, running steps in order, while CDK and Pulumi are declarative
questions.why: All of them end up declarative: you describe desired state and the tool diffs it against reality. Terraform uses HCL; CDK and Pulumi let you build that description with loops, functions and types in TypeScript, C# or Python, and both still preview changes.
questions.asked: Tool-choice question; strong answers note that 'real code' also makes it easier to be too clever.

questions.q: In IaC, what does it mean for an operation to be idempotent?
choices: Every apply destroys and recreates all the resources, so each run starts from a clean slate
The tool refuses to run twice in one day, to avoid duplicate resources
The same configuration may produce different results depending on timing
Applying the same configuration again makes no changes once reality matches it
questions.why: Declarative tools compare desired and actual state and only act on the difference, so re-running an apply is safe. A script of imperative 'create' calls, by contrast, fails or duplicates resources when run twice.
questions.asked: Explains why declarative IaC beats a bash script of CLI commands.

questions.q: A new developer asks why your team does not just use one cloud account for dev, staging and production. What is the strongest reason?
choices: Separate accounts isolate permissions, quotas and blast radius per environment
Providers charge less per resource when the same services are split across accounts
One account can hold only one database, so each environment needs its own
Dev resources in a production account are deleted automatically every night
questions.why: Account (or subscription/project) boundaries are the hardest isolation the cloud offers: a dev credential cannot touch production, a runaway test cannot exhaust production quotas, and billing splits cleanly. There is no per-account discount or one-database limit.
questions.asked: Shows awareness of environment isolation beyond naming conventions.

questions.q: Your managed Postgres instance hits 100% of its provisioned storage. What typically happens?
choices: The provider silently deletes the oldest rows to make room for new writes
Writes fail or the instance becomes read-only until storage is increased
Storage overflows into object storage and queries slow down but keep working
