The instance fails over to its standby, which has twice the storage available
questions.why: A full disk stops the database from writing data and WAL, so writes fail and the instance may enter a storage-full state. Enable storage autoscaling where offered and alert well before the limit; the standby has the same size.
questions.asked: A classic avoidable outage; interviewers want alerting and autoscaling in the answer.

questions.q: Your managed database performance drops sharply every afternoon, though CPU and memory look fine. The disk IOPS graph is flat at a ceiling. What does that suggest?
choices: The database has too many indexes, so it should drop all of them at once
The connection pool is too large, which caps IOPS for each client connection
You are hitting the storage tier's provisioned IOPS or throughput limit
The CDN is caching database pages, which throttles the underlying disk
questions.why: Cloud disks have IOPS and throughput caps (sometimes burst credits that run out), and a flat line at the cap is the tell. Raise provisioned IOPS, move to a faster tier, or cut I/O with better indexes and less scanning.
questions.asked: Reading a flat-topped graph correctly is a real skill; strong answers mention burst credits.

questions.q: Why is `0.0.0.0/0` on port 22 or 3389 in a security group a red flag?
choices: It blocks all SSH or RDP traffic, locking administrators out of the machine
It only allows traffic from other instances within the same availability zone
It routes all internet traffic through the instance, which then acts as a NAT
It exposes remote login to the whole internet, inviting scanning and brute force
questions.why: `0.0.0.0/0` means any IPv4 address. Admin access should go through a bastion, a VPN, session-manager style tooling or at least a narrow source range, and many teams remove SSH entirely in favour of immutable instances.
questions.asked: Classic misconfiguration from security reviews; interviewers want the alternatives.

questions.q: What is the practical difference between a public subnet and a private subnet?
choices: A public subnet routes to an internet gateway; a private one has no direct route in
A public subnet is shared with other customers, while a private one is dedicated to you
Public subnets are free to use, while private subnets are billed per hour of use
Public subnets allow only HTTP traffic, while private ones allow any protocol
questions.why: The route table decides it: a subnet whose default route points at an internet gateway is public, so resources with public IPs there are reachable. Load balancers go public; app servers and databases go private.
questions.asked: Foundation for any cloud architecture sketch; strong answers place each component.

questions.q: A CDN sits in front of your API. Which endpoint is a safe candidate for edge caching?
choices: `POST /orders`, since orders are created the same way for every customer
`GET /products?category=shoes` returning public catalogue data for a few seconds
`GET /me/orders`, provided the CDN caches by URL alone to save origin load
`DELETE /cart/items/5`, since repeating a delete is idempotent anyway
questions.why: Public, identical-for-everyone GET responses can be cached briefly at the edge, even for a few seconds, which absorbs spikes. Per-user responses cached by URL alone leak between users, and non-GET methods are not cacheable.
questions.asked: Tests judgement about what is cacheable; strong answers mention short TTLs and stale-while-revalidate.

questions.q: What is an origin shield (or tiered cache) in a CDN?
choices: A firewall rule that stops attackers from discovering the IP address of your origin server
A TLS certificate the CDN presents to your origin to prove its identity
A mid-tier cache that edge locations fetch through, cutting requests to your origin
A feature that serves a static error page when the origin is unavailable
questions.why: Without a shield, every edge location misses and hits your origin separately; with one, they fetch through a single regional cache, so a new object is fetched from origin roughly once. It protects origin capacity on cache misses and purges.
questions.asked: Shows deeper CDN knowledge; relevant when a purge causes an origin traffic spike.

questions.q: You purge the whole CDN cache after every deploy. What side effect should you expect?
choices: Users see the old version for a longer time, since purges are queued for a day
The CDN bills a one-off fee that equals the site's monthly bandwidth charge
The TLS certificate is revoked and has to be reissued for the domain
A burst of cache misses hits the origin at once until the cache refills
questions.why: A full purge turns every edge into a miss simultaneously, so the origin takes the full load right after a deploy. Content-hashed asset names avoid most purging, and targeted purges or an origin shield soften the rest.
questions.asked: Cause-and-effect reasoning about caches; a good follow-up to hashed filenames.

questions.q: In a cloud console, you see an object storage bucket flagged as 'public'. What should you do first?
choices: Confirm whether it is meant to be public, then enable block-public-access if not
Delete the bucket immediately, since public buckets are always a security breach
Rename the bucket so that the old public URL no longer resolves to its contents
Enable versioning, which makes existing objects private again automatically
questions.why: Some buckets legitimately serve public assets, so check intent before acting; then block public access at bucket or account level and review what was exposed. Deleting destroys evidence and data, and versioning does not change permissions.
questions.asked: Public buckets are the most famous cloud leak; strong answers mention account-level guardrails.

questions.q: Your team uses a managed Kubernetes service. Which part do you still operate yourself?
choices: The etcd cluster that stores the Kubernetes control-plane state and its backups
Your workloads' manifests, resource limits, node pools and upgrade timing
The Kubernetes API server's availability, which you run on your own VMs
The physical networking between the provider's data centres and regions
questions.why: Managed Kubernetes runs the control plane for you, but you still own deployments, requests and limits, scaling, node pool versions and upgrades, and everything inside the cluster. It is less managed than a PaaS such as Cloud Run or App Service.
questions.asked: Helps calibrate 'should we use Kubernetes'; strong answers compare it with simpler PaaS options.

questions.q: A team wants to host a single CRUD API with modest traffic. Which reasoning about Kubernetes is most sound?
choices: Kubernetes is required for any containerised app, so it should be used from day one
Kubernetes is always cheaper than a PaaS, because it packs containers tightly
A PaaS or managed container service is simpler until you need Kubernetes' features
Kubernetes cannot run a single API, since it needs at least ten services to schedule
questions.why: Kubernetes pays off with many services, custom scheduling or a platform team to run it; for one API it adds upgrades, networking and YAML to own. Containers run happily on Cloud Run, App Service, Fly.io or ECS without it.
questions.asked: Judgement question; interviewers like candidates who resist over-engineering.

questions.q: Cloud providers publish an SLA of, say, 99.95% for a managed service. What does the SLA actually give you if it is breached?
choices: Automatic compensation for your lost revenue during the outage period
A guarantee that the outage will not happen again for the next twelve months
Free migration to a different region chosen by the provider's engineers
Service credits on your bill, usually a percentage of that service's cost
questions.why: SLA remedies are credits against the service's own charge, which rarely match your business loss. The SLA tells you what to design around, not what you will be paid; your own availability target must account for it.
questions.asked: Corrects the common belief that an SLA is insurance.

questions.q: How does a cloud provider's DDoS protection typically help a public web app?
choices: It absorbs and filters volumetric floods at the network edge before they reach you
It rate-limits every user to one request per second so floods are impossible
It moves your app to a secret IP address each time an attack is detected
It blocks all traffic from countries outside your home region automatically
questions.why: Providers have edge capacity far beyond any single app, so network-layer floods are dropped there; CDNs and WAF rate rules help with application-layer floods. Per-user limits of one request per second would break normal browsing.
questions.asked: Basic edge-security awareness; strong answers separate network-layer from application-layer attacks.

questions.q: Your web app, API and database are in one availability zone. A zone outage takes everything down. What is the minimum change to survive it?
choices: Add a second region with its own database, and fail over between them by hand
Run app instances in two or more zones and use a multi-AZ database
Increase the instance sizes, since larger instances are placed in several zones
Take backups every hour, so you can rebuild quickly after the zone returns
questions.why: Spreading instances across zones behind the load balancer, plus a multi-AZ database, survives a single-zone failure within one region. Multi-region is far more complex and costly; backups help recovery but not availability.
questions.asked: Right-sized reliability; interviewers like 'multi-AZ first, multi-region only if the business needs it'.

questions.q: What is the purpose of a CAA DNS record?
choices: It points the domain at the certificate authority's servers for validation
It publishes the site's public key so browsers can skip the TLS handshake
It lists which certificate authorities may issue certificates for the domain
It tells browsers to always use HTTPS for the domain, like an HSTS header
questions.why: Certificate Authority Authorization records restrict issuance: a CA must check them and refuse if it is not listed, reducing the risk of a rogue certificate. HSTS is a separate HTTP header, and CAA does not affect the handshake.
questions.asked: A niche but telling detail; it tends to come up when a certificate renewal is unexpectedly refused.

questions.q: Your app serves over HTTPS, but the first visit to `http://example.com` is still redirected via plain HTTP. What does HSTS add?
choices: It encrypts the plain-HTTP redirect response itself so that it cannot be read in transit
It moves the redirect into DNS so no HTTP request is ever made at all
It makes the load balancer reject port 80, so HTTP requests fail instead
After a first HTTPS visit, the browser upgrades future requests to HTTPS itself
questions.why: `Strict-Transport-Security` tells the browser to use HTTPS for the domain for `max-age`, so later visits never send plain HTTP that an attacker could intercept. The very first visit stays exposed unless the domain is on the browser preload list.
questions.asked: Shows you understand the SSL-stripping risk that a redirect alone does not solve.

questions.q: Your production database was created by hand in the console before the team adopted Terraform. How do you bring it under IaC without recreating it?
choices: Delete it and let Terraform create a fresh one, then restore last night's backup
Write the matching resource block and import the existing resource into state
Copy its settings into a tfvars file, since Terraform reads state from variables
Nothing is needed, because Terraform discovers every resource in the account
questions.why: An import (the `import` block or `terraform import`) records the real resource's id in state against your resource block; then `plan` should show no changes once the code matches. Deleting and restoring causes downtime and data loss, and Terraform only manages what is in its state.
questions.asked: Almost every team adopts IaC with existing resources; knowing import shows you have done it.
